en: Śroṇa,
Śāriputra said this to him: "Śroṇa, whatever ascetics or brahmins [regard] form as impermanent, unstable, unreliable, and subject to change— "

“They think, ‘We are superior,’ they think, ‘We are equal,’ or they think, ‘We are inferior’; it is nowhere else, Śoṇa, that these ascetics or brahmins [hold such views] because of their failure to see things as they truly are.
Whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be, Śoṇa, who [regard] feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent,”
By means of consciousness— which is unstable, unreliable, and subject to change— those [ascetics] think, "We are superior," they think,
"We are equal," or they think, "We are inferior. It is solely because they do not see things as they truly are, Śroṇa, that those ascetics or brahmins think in such a way.
But those ascetics or brahmins, Śroṇa, who— regarding form that is impermanent, unstable, unreliable, and subject to change—
do not think "we are superior," do not think "we are equal," and do not think "we are inferior," [they do so] because,
Śroṇa, those ascetics or brahmins [do not rely] on anything other than feeling, perception, and mental formations, which are impermanent.

Śroṇa, those ascetics or brahmins do not think, "We are superior" because of their consciousness— which is impermanent, unstable, unreliable, and subject to change— nor do they think, "We are equal," nor do they think, "We are inferior"; rather, it is solely from seeing things as they truly are that they [attain this state].
"What do you think, Śroṇa, is form permanent or impermanent?
"It is impermanent, venerable Śāriputra.
"And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering? Even though it is subject to change, would a learned noble disciple regard it as a self, thinking: 'This is mine; this am I'?"
"This is my self," [he said].
"No, indeed, Śāriputra.
"What do you think, Śroṇa? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?"

"O Śāriputra, this is impermanent. Now, that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—would a learned noble disciple regard it as a self, thinking: 'This is mine, this am I, this is my self'?
"No, Venerable Śāriputra."
Therefore, Śroṇa, whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external;
gross or subtle; inferior or superior; whether far or near—all that should be seen as it truly is with correct wisdom: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
Therefore, Śroṇa, whatever feeling, perception, mental formations, or whatever consciousness there may be—whether past, future, or present;

internal or external; gross or subtle—as before, up until: ... the noble disciple, having become weary even of form, becomes weary of feeling, perception, mental formations, and even of consciousness; being weary, he...

"One becomes dispassionate; being dispassionate, one is liberated; for one who is liberated, the knowledge arises: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, I know there is no further state of existence beyond this. While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dharma arose in Śroṇa, the son of a householder, regarding all phenomena.
Then Śroṇa, the householder’s son, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma—

having crossed over doubt, transcended uncertainty, and attained fearlessness in the matters of the teachings— rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Venerable Śāriputra, he addressed the Venerable Śāriputra as follows:

"I have transcended, Venerable Śāriputra, I have truly transcended! Just as I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks, please accept me from this day forward as a lay follower for as long as life shall last. Śroṇa, the son of a householder, having rejoiced and approved of what the Venerable Śāriputra had said, bowed his head at the feet of the Venerable Śāriputra.
Having paid homage, he departed from the presence of the venerable Śāriputra.
